question: Are these groups that having lost Aleppo might align with the so-called Islamic State elsewhere in Syria, or are they distinct and different and opposed to that group?
true_answer_verbatim: I think that anyone who considers himself a Syrian nationalist - in essence a Syria-firster - would find it very, very, very difficult to sign up with ISIS because ISIS of course believes it has a worldwide mission. And ISIS really has not been engaged in fighting Bashar al-Assad very much in any event.
true_answer_paraphrased: I think that anyone who considers himself a Syrian nationalist, essentially someone who puts Syria first, would find it extremely difficult to join ISIS because ISIS believes it has a worldwide mission. And ISIS has not been fighting Bashar al-Assad very much.

options.text: After the collapse in eastern Aleppo, those defeated brigades have no choice. I expect thousands of fighters will retreat toward Raqqa and pledge allegiance to Daesh simply to survive the bombing campaigns by Russian jets and Hezbollah militias.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that the defeated groups will not join ISIS due to ideological differences, whereas Answer 2 asserts that they will pledge allegiance to ISIS out of a need to survive.

options.text: I think that anyone who considers himself a Syrian nationalist, essentially someone who puts Syria first, would find it extremely difficult to join ISIS because ISIS believes it has a worldwide mission. And ISIS has not been fighting Bashar al-Assad very much.

I believe we will see a large merger. Hardline groups like Ahrar al-Sham already share strong Salafist roots with Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi’s network. Losing their urban stronghold accelerates their inevitable integration into the Caliphate across Idlib and the Euphrates valley.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that the groups will not join the Islamic State due to ideological differences, whereas Answer 2 asserts that they will inevitably merge with the group due to shared extremist roots.

options.text: The Free Syrian Army units in the Levant are out of money. With the CIA freezing covert support, many commanders will defect to the Islamic State in Deir ez-Zor, drawn by the oil smuggling wealth and heavy artillery there.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that the rebel groups will not join the Islamic State due to ideological differences, whereas Answer 2 asserts that they will defect to the Islamic State for financial and material reasons.
